strengths: Originality/significance: FLEXRANK offers a compelling train-once approach to extracting nested, low-rank submodels from pretrained networks. Combining data-aware factorization, global rank allocation, nested distillation, and shared parameters is useful for heterogeneous deployment.

Soundness: The linear-matrix analysis gives meaningful intuition for why arbitrary submodel sampling can cause interference and why prefix-nested components are compatible. The PTS, ASL, and NSL controlled experiment in Figure 2 supports this analysis.

Empirical scope: The evaluation spans GPT-2, three Llama sizes up to 8B, and DINOv3 models up to 7B. Figures 4–5 show substantially smoother accuracy degradation than SVD/DataSVD, while Figure 3 provides a valuable small-scale exhaustive comparison against independently trained configurations.

The ablations examine several important components, including activation sample count, end-to-end versus layerwise training, nonuniform layer allocation, and joint nested-submodel training. The post-adaptation LoRA experiment also suggests that compressed submodels retain useful downstream adaptability.

Presentation: The motivation, three-stage method, and nestedness intuition are generally clear. The paper openly acknowledges the strong additive-error approximation, substantial distillation cost, limited training schedule, and absence of input-adaptive evaluation.

Reproducibility is partially supported by named datasets, architectures, evaluation tasks, optimizer settings, batch sizes, sequence length, step counts, and an informative accounting of the large-scale compute used.
weaknesses: The central practical claim is not adequately demonstrated: results use relative parameter count rather than measured latency, throughput, peak memory, energy, or FLOPs on actual hardware. Low-rank factorization can be kernel- and shape-dependent, and Section 3.5 supplies only an asymptotic argument. Consequently, the claimed performance-latency Pareto frontier and adaptive-deployment benefit remain unsupported empirically.

The theory does not establish the principal deep-network claims. The results apply to a single linear matrix with squared reconstruction loss and ideal global optimization. FLEXRANK instead relies on independently factorized nonlinear layers, additive layer errors, a fixed configuration ordering that is assumed to survive distillation, and stochastic optimization. No bound connects these approximations to Pareto optimality in transformers, yet the manuscript repeatedly calls the practical rank choices or submodels Pareto-optimal.

Baseline coverage and fairness are insufficient for the broad claim of outperforming state-of-the-art compression and elasticity approaches. Large-scale plots compare mainly against SVD variants and ACIP; flexible-model methods such as MatFormer, Flextron, and LlamaFlex are discussed but not evaluated. Strong trained low-rank methods listed in Table 2 are also absent from the main curves. It is unclear whether baseline repair methods receive compute, data, and tuning comparable to FLEXRANK's costly multi-billion-token full-model distillation.

The empirical reporting is too incomplete to verify the headline results. Figures 4–5 provide curves without numerical tables, uncertainty, per-task scores, or repeated-run information. The small exhaustive MNIST experiment lacks sufficient architectural and optimization details, and the main comparisons do not report statistical variation.

Several essential implementation choices are missing: the number and spacing of budget levels, sampling weights alpha_k, precise distillation loss and temperature, ranks allowed per layer, layers excluded from factorization, sensitivity metric and DP discretization, calibration/probing protocol, and baseline hyperparameters. No code or artifact is identified. These omissions materially limit reproducibility.

The paper conflates calibration and training requirements. Section 3 suggests a representative calibration set of roughly 10^3 samples, whereas the reported LLM refinement uses 10,000 steps with batch size 512 and length 1024—roughly 5.2 billion token positions—and Appendix D reports up to 384 A100-GPU-days for the 8B model. Thus, the practical advantage over training or maintaining several models needs a quantitative amortization analysis.

The formal setup has presentation defects: Definition 2.1 does not clearly enforce comparison at equal or lower cost and mixes maximized performance with earlier minimization notation; Equation 4 is described as finding a Pareto front although it minimizes a sum over predetermined budgets; and the claim following Theorem 4.1 that any algorithm optimizing the full-model objective has zero probability of finding a suitable factorization is stronger than the measure-zero statement without a justified distribution over attained global minimizers.

The limitations section is honest but incomplete. It mentions additional training and missing input adaptivity, but not the lack of real-system efficiency measurements, limited baseline comparison, dependence on large proxy data, or possible degradation outside the selected budgets/tasks. The generic impact statement also overlooks inherited bias and licensing/privacy considerations associated with distillation from pretrained models and web-scale proxy data.

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem: obtaining many compute/parameter budgets from one pretrained model and one shared parameter set.

FLEXRANK is an intuitive combination of activation-aware low-rank initialization, global rank allocation, nested weight sharing, and teacher distillation. Applying nested low-rank training at LLM and large-ViT scale appears reasonably original.

The reported parameter–accuracy curves are promising and span GPT-2, three Llama models, and DINOv3 models up to 7B parameters. The controlled MNIST experiment and GPT-2 ablations help isolate initialization, end-to-end training, and submodel sampling.
The linear analysis provides useful intuition for why arbitrary factorized solutions need not yield good truncations and why compatible nested objectives can avoid interference.

The manuscript is generally organized and visually clear. It also candidly reports substantial training costs and acknowledges limited training, missing input adaptivity, and the possible need for improved optimization.
No major application-specific ethical risk is apparent beyond the usual risks of inherited teacher-model behavior and substantial compute consumption.
weaknesses: The central theoretical narrative is materially overstated. Theorem 4.1 establishes, at most, that favorable factorizations form a measure-zero subset of the global-minimizer manifold. It does not show that an algorithm cannot deliberately select that subset—SVD does exactly this. Moreover, the proof assumes without justification that a continuous random initialization induces an absolutely continuous distribution over the final gauge transformation after gradient descent. Thus the paper's claim that post-training selection, or even “any algorithm” optimizing the full model, fails with probability one is unsupported.

The theory does not justify the practical algorithm on deep nonlinear networks. The guarantees concern one linear matrix, exact global optimization, all ranks, and squared reconstruction loss. FLEXRANK instead fixes masks obtained from independently probed layers under an additive-error assumption and performs stochastic distillation. Neither the additivity assumption nor preservation of the selected ordering during training is established. The latter is only tested on a small MNIST network, despite being the method's central approximation.

There are apparent proof-level inconsistencies in Appendix B. For example, the genericity argument around Eq. (50) treats the zero set as a proper codimension-one subspace for every r, although the displayed expression is identically zero at r=k. More broadly, its substitution for lambda is not derived from the nonlinear consistency condition in Lemma B.6. These issues weaken confidence in Theorem 4.2's claimed generic strict-gap conclusion.

The advertised deployment and performance–latency Pareto claims are not evaluated. Experiments report parameter counts, not measured latency, throughput, peak memory, energy, or hardware-specific break-even points. Two low-rank matrix multiplications can be slower than one dense multiplication because of kernel and memory overhead, so parameter reduction alone does not establish practical adaptive computation.

The empirical comparison is too narrow for the broad state-of-the-art claim. Main LLM results compare primarily with SVD/DataSVD and ACIP; several listed trainable low-rank methods are absent, while relevant elastic approaches such as MatFormer, Flextron, and LlamaFlex are excluded because they use a different mechanism. Mechanism is not a sufficient reason to omit competitors when the claimed contribution is adaptive deployment. Vision experiments have no trained elastic baseline at all.

Comparison fairness and statistical reliability are unclear. The paper does not provide matched training data, optimization budget, or tuning details for ACIP; main curves contain no uncertainty estimates or exact values; results are averaged across heterogeneous commonsense tasks without per-task reporting; and the number of training runs or seeds is unspecified. Table 1's ± values are not explained and cannot substitute for run-to-run variability.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code or artifact availability is stated, and important details are missing: the precise distillation loss and temperature, number and spacing of configurations, sampling weights alpha_k, rank candidates, dynamic-programming recurrence and discretization, method for enforcing nestedness jointly across budgets, handling of embeddings and tied weights, and exact evaluation settings. The asserted O(LK) dynamic-programming complexity is also insufficiently supported for a multi-choice knapsack problem with both rank choices and budget states.

The method is computationally expensive despite the framing of lightweight reuse: the authors report up to 64 A100 GPUs for six days and training on roughly 5.2B token positions. A careful total-cost comparison against independently compressing or training a practical number of target models is missing, so the amortization benefit of “train once, deploy everywhere” is not demonstrated.

The paper repeatedly uses “true Pareto front,” “Pareto optimal,” and “consistently outperforms state of the art” more strongly than the evidence permits. The real-model experiments do not enumerate the attainable model space, compare against all relevant alternatives, or measure deployment cost; they therefore demonstrate favorable parameter–accuracy curves, not a true global Pareto frontier.

The limitations and impact discussions are too cursory. They do not adequately discuss the strong proxy-data requirement, possible distribution shift in rank allocation, inherited bias and safety behavior across compressed submodels, or the environmental cost of the reported compute. These omissions are not themselves the primary rejection reason, but should be addressed.

strengths: Originality: FLEXRANK offers a novel and coherent combination of data-aware layer factorization, globally nested rank allocation, and joint distillation, yielding many budget-specific models from shared weights.

Soundness: The linear-model analysis clearly distinguishes post-training selection, all-subspace learning, and nested learning. The nested-learning result is intuitive and, in its stated linear setting, supports the central design choice.

Empirical scope: Results cover GPT-2, three Llama models up to 8B parameters, and DINOv3 vision transformers up to 7B. The reported accuracy-versus-size curves show unusually graceful degradation, including strong ImageNet performance at aggressive compression.
Significance: A single model supporting many deployment budgets is practically useful, and factor-space elasticity complements architectural slicing, pruning, and quantization.
The controlled exhaustive experiment, component-wise rank profiles, initialization study, and sampling ablations provide useful evidence beyond the headline comparisons.
Presentation is generally clear and well organized, with a helpful overview, explicit objectives, proofs, resource estimates, and an honest discussion of limited training and input adaptivity.
No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the work may reduce repeated training and deployment costs, although its impact statement is generic.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theory applies to a single linear matrix and does not establish that the layerwise probing, additive-error approximation, or fixed rank assignments recover a Pareto frontier in deep nonlinear networks. The manuscript sometimes presents this limited result as broader theoretical support for FLEXRANK.

The formalization is internally inconsistent about whether R is a loss or a higher-is-better performance measure: Equation 1 minimizes R, whereas Definition 2.1 uses a greater-than comparison to define domination.

Theorem 4.1 only shows that suitable factorizations form a measure-zero subset of all exact factorizations; it does not justify the stronger prose claim that any algorithm optimizing only the full model has zero chance of finding one, since an algorithm can explicitly select an SVD-aligned gauge.

The ASL appendix overstates generic strict positivity for every rank. Its derivation substitutes lambda with the mean target singular value without handling inactive thresholded singular values, and the displayed bound can be zero at full rank. This does not invalidate the core nested-learning theorem but weakens the surrounding claims.

The main evidence reports parameter count rather than measured latency, throughput, memory, or energy on actual hardware. Consequently, claims about a performance-latency Pareto frontier and practical adaptive deployment are not directly demonstrated. Budget-specific gauge transformations used for the proposed inference optimization are also not benchmarked.

Baseline coverage is limited: ACIP is the only trained elastic low-rank competitor in the main language-model plots, vision experiments compare only against untrained SVD variants, and no architectural elastic methods are evaluated. Excluding such methods because they are not low-rank is understandable mechanistically but weakens the broad claim of outperforming compression and elasticity approaches.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives broad hyperparameters and hardware costs but no code, seeds, number of runs, rank-grid size, sampling weights alpha_k, detailed distillation loss, DP recurrence, or sufficient baseline-training details. The claimed O(LK) multi-choice-knapsack complexity is asserted without enough algorithmic detail and appears optimistic when each layer has K choices.

DataSVD requires an inverse covariance square root, yet the covariance is rank deficient when the stated calibration sample count is smaller than a layer width; pseudoinverse or regularization details are omitted.

Most main results lack uncertainty estimates and per-task values. Aggregate commonsense accuracy can conceal regressions, while Table 1 does not explain whether its intervals reflect seeds or evaluation uncertainty.

The training cost remains substantial—up to 32 A100 GPUs for six days for the 8B model—and no quantitative comparison with independently producing several compressed models is provided. Thus, the practical meaning of “train once” and the break-even point are unclear.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges incomplete optimization and missing input-adaptive evaluation, but it should also discuss the unvalidated additivity assumption, absence of hardware measurements, restricted baseline coverage, calibration-data requirements, and considerable distillation cost.

strengths: Originality/significance: FLEXRANK presents a useful combination of data-aware low-rank initialization, globally allocated nested ranks, joint distillation, and an inference-time reparameterization. A single shared model supporting many deployment budgets is practically important.

Soundness: The empirical study is unusually broad, covering GPT-2, three Llama sizes up to 8B, and DINOv3 models up to 7B. The reported curves consistently favor FLEXRANK over SVD/DataSVD and ACIP, and the GPT-2 ablations separately examine initialization, end-to-end consolidation, and budget sampling.

The controlled linear analysis gives a helpful conceptual explanation of why nested prefixes can avoid interference between same-rank submodels. The exhaustive small-scale ranking experiment also directly tests the additive-probe assumption, reporting Spearman correlation 0.991, a 3.7% violation rate, and 94.1% exact-budget agreement.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized, motivates elasticity clearly, distinguishes calibration/search/consolidation/deployment stages, and includes pseudocode and an honest discussion of training overhead.

Practical relevance: Applying GAR uniformly to rank-based baselines is a sensible comparison choice, and the paper includes an actual GPU runtime experiment rather than relying exclusively on parameter or FLOP counts.

Ethics/limitations: The paper acknowledges dependence on representative training data, consolidation compute, factorized-training overhead, and the absence of adaptive-routing evaluation. No major unresolved ethical concern is apparent for the proposed compression method.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed O(LK) dynamic-programming complexity is not supported by Algorithms 2–3. EXPANDLAYER forms the Cartesian product of the current frontier and every candidate for the next layer; the frontier can grow with the number of attainable savings and can be exponential without discretization or a proved size bound. PARETOPRUNE and the final greedy NESTEDCHAIN do not establish that the resulting chain optimizes the jointly nested problem in Eq. (4). This is central to the claimed scalable, near-optimal rank selection.

Soundness: GAR assumes that an r-by-r row block of U is invertible. This need not hold, and near-singularity can make the transformed factors numerically unstable. The paper neither specifies pivoting/permutation to select a nonsingular well-conditioned block nor evaluates conditioning or numerical error. Thus the unconditional claim that GAR provides the stated deployable realization is insufficiently justified.

Theory: The probabilistic conclusion in the proof of Theorem 4.1 assumes that a continuously distributed initialization induces an absolutely continuous distribution over the gauge R reached by optimization. Assumptions B.1–B.2 do not imply this; an optimizer's implicit bias could map many initializations to a measure-zero canonical factorization. The measure-zero geometric statement is plausible, but the stronger claim about what training finds is not proved.

Theory: The proof following Theorem 4.2 substitutes lambda as the mean of the target singular values in Eq. (52), although Lemma B.6 defines lambda through thresholded values w_i=max(0,2 sigma_i-lambda). That substitution is invalid when any w_i is zero, a case allowed by the theorem. This undermines the stated generic positive-gap argument. More broadly, the exact linear-matrix results do not justify Pareto optimality for nonlinear deep networks.

Evaluation: Most main results are curves without numerical tables, uncertainty, seeds, or statistical testing. Table 1 reports plus/minus values without defining whether they are variation across runs, tasks, or sampling error. It is therefore difficult to assess robustness or the size of several gains.

Evaluation: The independent-submodel baseline gives each of ten models only 10% of FLEXRANK's total updates. This matches aggregate compute but does not establish comparison with independently converged models, so it cannot substantiate repeated claims that the shared model recovers or exceeds the true Pareto frontier at scale.

Evaluation: Deployment is primarily evaluated by relative parameter count. The sole runtime study uses one synthetic 4096-by-4096 layer, one long token count, one RTX 5090, and torch.compile; it does not demonstrate end-to-end latency, memory, or throughput improvements for the evaluated Llama and DINOv3 models across hardware or batch/sequence regimes.

Reproducibility: Important details are missing or ambiguous, including the number and exact grid of rank candidates, budget-sampling weights alpha_k, the precise distillation loss and temperature, some optimizer settings, DP cost discretization, GAR pivot handling, seeds, and complete details for the controlled MNIST/DNN experiment. The manuscript's code link is not usable in the provided version.

Presentation: The formal Pareto definition is inconsistent with surrounding notation: Eq. (1) minimizes R although R is subsequently treated as performance to maximize, and Definition 2.1 compares only performance under a budget constraint rather than standard cost-performance dominance. Terms such as 'true Pareto front' and 'Pareto-optimal' are consequently used more strongly than the demonstrated evidence supports.

Significance is limited by the substantial 5B-token teacher-distillation requirement, roughly 2x factorized-training memory/latency overhead, and the need to train separate LoRA adapters for each downstream submodel. These qualifications weaken the advertised 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' interpretation. The generic impact statement also omits discussion of these energy costs and of risks inherited from the teacher/proxy data.

strengths: Originality/significance: FLEXRANK combines data-aware low-rank initialization, globally allocated nested ranks, joint distillation, and an inference-time reparameterization into a potentially useful train-once/deploy-at-many-budgets framework. Applying this idea across GPT-2, three Llama sizes, and DINOv3 models up to 7B parameters is ambitious.

Soundness: The linear-matrix analysis provides useful intuition for why arbitrary factor truncation can fail and why prefix-nested components are compatible with truncated-SVD solutions. The comparison with independently trained submodels is also a valuable attempt to isolate the effect of weight sharing.

Empirical merit: The reported accuracy curves are consistently favorable relative to SVD, DataSVD, and ACIP, with additional downstream adaptation experiments and ablations concerning calibration size, submodel sampling, and layerwise versus end-to-end training.

Presentation: The high-level pipeline is understandable, the paper openly identifies its additive-error assumption, approximately 2x training-memory overhead, slower factorized training, dependence on proxy data, and lack of adaptive-routing evaluation. These honest limitations should not themselves be penalized.
weaknesses: Soundness: The dynamic program is presented as selecting near-optimal nested configurations, but its guarantee rests on additive layer errors and fixed ranking preservation. This crucial assumption is tested only on one tiny exhaustively searchable problem. More seriously, the descriptions of that problem conflict: Section 3.4 describes a four-layer CNN/MLP experiment on MNIST with 10,000 configurations, Figure 2 refers to 1,023 submodels, Appendix C.3 again says MNIST with 10^4 submodels, while Appendix D.1 specifies a two-linear-layer synthetic Gaussian regression problem. This makes the central validation impossible to interpret or reproduce.

Soundness: Algorithms 2–3 do not establish the claimed O(LK) complexity or optimal nested solution. Expanding every current frontier state with every layer candidate is generally quadratic in the frontier/candidate count, and NESTEDCHAIN greedily filters a previously computed Pareto set rather than optimizing the nested chain objective in Equation 4. No proof is supplied that this filtering yields the best jointly nested profiles.

Soundness: The theoretical results concern a single linear matrix with a Frobenius reconstruction objective, whereas FLEXRANK operates across interacting nonlinear layers and task losses. The manuscript repeatedly uses this limited result to explain deep-network behavior and Pareto optimality without a justified bridge. Moreover, the proof of Theorem 4.2 treats lambda as the mean target singular value in Equation 52, although Lemma B.6 defines it implicitly after thresholding; that algebra is invalid when some optimized singular values are zero. The probability argument in the proof of Theorem 4.1 also assumes, without justification, that random initialization induces an absolutely continuous distribution over the converged gauge.

Evidence/significance: The central deployment claim is based mostly on parameter count, not end-to-end latency, throughput, peak memory, or energy. GAR is benchmarked only for one isolated 4096-by-4096 multiplication with 8,192 tokens on an RTX 5090. There are no complete-model measurements across the claimed Llama/ViT budgets or heterogeneous devices. GAR additionally requires an invertible selected row block and may be numerically unstable; existence, pivoting, conditioning, and accuracy after the transformation are not analyzed.

Evaluation: Main results are curves without numerical tables, uncertainty estimates, or reported repetitions. Averaging six language tasks can hide regressions, and the paper does not provide per-task results. Comparisons outside low-rank methods are restricted to one 1B model and use methods at differing training recipes; statements such as being competitive beyond rank-based approaches are consequently weak. Important elastic baselines such as MatFormer/Flextron/LlamaFlex are discussed but not evaluated.

Reproducibility: The manuscript omits essential details including the exact distillation loss and temperature, profile-sampling weights, rank candidate grids, which modules are factorized, calibration construction and size for each model, random seeds, optimizer weight decay, full training compute, and baseline tuning procedures. The displayed code link is empty, and the internally inconsistent controlled-experiment specification compounds the problem.

Presentation: Claims such as recovering the “true Pareto front,” obtaining “Pareto-optimal” deep submodels, and “deploy everywhere” are substantially stronger than the evidence. At most, the experiments identify a frontier within a restricted family and show favorable parameter–accuracy trade-offs; they do not establish global Pareto optimality or broadly realized deployment efficiency.

Research ethics and limitations: No acute ethical issue is apparent, but the impact statement is boilerplate and does not discuss how cheaper deployment may broaden both beneficial and harmful uses of the underlying models. The limitations section is helpful but omits the most material threats: weak validation of rank preservation, GAR conditioning, lack of end-to-end deployment measurements, and limited statistical reporting. Overall, the promising idea and scale do not overcome unresolved issues in the central optimization claims, theoretical argument, experimental specification, and deployment evidence.

strengths: Originality/significance: FLEXRANK combines activation-aware low-rank initialization, globally nested rank allocation, joint distillation, and gauge-aligned reparameterization into a compelling train-once/deploy-at-many-budgets framework. The ability to extract many configurations from shared weights addresses a practically important deployment problem.

Soundness: The linear analysis clearly distinguishes post-training selection, all-subspace learning, and nested-subspace learning. Theorems 4.1–4.3 and the synthetic experiments provide useful insight into why nested objectives can avoid interference, with assumptions and proofs stated in the appendix.

Empirical breadth: Experiments cover GPT-2, three Llama sizes up to 8B, and DINOv3 models up to 7B. Figure 4 shows substantially smoother degradation than SVD, DataSVD, and ACIP across many parameter budgets, especially for the vision models.

The ablations are informative: the paper separately examines DataSVD calibration size, end-to-end versus layerwise consolidation, budget sampling, learned layerwise rank profiles, and independently trained submodels. These experiments support the main design choices rather than presenting only aggregate gains.

Presentation: The motivation, algorithmic stages, and relationship between nestedness and elasticity are generally clear. The paper also gives a candid limitations discussion covering proxy-data dependence, training overhead, lack of adaptive-routing evaluation, and unfused factorized kernels.

Reproducibility/ethics: Algorithms, decompositions, optimization schedules, datasets, evaluation tasks, and core hyperparameters are substantially documented. The work poses limited direct ethical risk and may reduce the resource cost of serving multiple model variants.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theoretical guarantees apply to a single linear matrix-reconstruction problem with distinct singular values and global minimizers. They do not establish Pareto optimality for deep nonlinear networks, knowledge distillation, or the DP-selected configurations. Accordingly, descriptions such as “Pareto optimal” or “recovers the true Pareto front” should be qualified outside the controlled setting.

A central approximation—the preservation of configuration rankings under additive per-layer errors—is validated only in a small exhaustively searchable setting. Although the reported Spearman correlation of 0.991 and 94.1% exact-budget success are encouraging, there is no corresponding validation on realistic Transformer architectures; interactions across many compressed layers could change the ordering after consolidation.

Reproducibility is weakened by an apparent inconsistency in the controlled-experiment description: Section 3.4 describes a four-layer setting involving two CNNs and two MLPs trained on MNIST, Appendix C.3 also refers to MNIST, whereas Appendix D.1 specifies a two-layer linear network on synthetic Gaussian data. It is consequently unclear which setup produced Figures 3 and 9.

The main large-model plots report single curves and averaged task accuracy without per-task results, repeated-run variability, or statistical tests. Table 1 includes uncertainty, but the source of that uncertainty is not explained. Exact numerical tables would also make the claimed improvements easier to verify.

The deployment evidence is incomplete. Parameter count is used as the main cost proxy, while the only runtime experiment is a single 4096-by-4096 matrix on one RTX 5090 with 8192 tokens. End-to-end latency, memory, throughput, and energy measurements across complete Llama and ViT submodels are needed to substantiate broad practical deployment claims.

Baseline coverage and compute matching are uneven. Non-low-rank compression methods are compared only on Llama-3.2-1B, several relevant elastic architectures are omitted, and choosing each method at its “best tuning/budget” is not a precise controlled-compute protocol. GAR is additionally supplied to all rank baselines, which is reasonable for isolating training quality but makes the comparison partly an evaluation of modified baselines.

Important implementation choices remain underspecified, including the budget set, sampling weights α_k, exact distillation loss, candidate-rank discretization, random seeds, and DP tie-breaking/frontier-size behavior. The stated O(LK) DP complexity also appears insufficiently justified by Algorithms 2–3, whose expansion cost depends on both the number of retained frontier states and candidates per layer.

The impact statement is perfunctory. While no major ethical concern is apparent, the paper should mention that compression may produce budget-dependent and subgroup-dependent reliability changes, particularly if adaptive routing is later used.
